title: new and delete
lesson:
Stack variables vanish when their function ends. Sometimes you need something to **outlive** the function that made it (a bullet fired in one frame that flies for the next fifty), or you only learn the size while running (how many sensor readings to keep). For that you ask the heap with `new`.

```
Bullet* b = new Bullet(10);   // one object on the heap; you get its address
b->damage;                    // use it through the pointer
delete b;                     // give it back
b = nullptr;                  // so nobody uses the old address

int* samples = new int[n];    // an array of n ints on the heap
samples[0] = 42;
delete[] samples;             // arrays use delete[]
```

**The rules.** Every `new` needs exactly one `delete`. Every `new[]` needs exactly one `delete[]`. Mixing them (`delete` on an array) is undefined behaviour. `delete nullptr` is allowed and does nothing.

**Three ways to get it wrong:**

- **Leak:** you forget `delete`. The memory stays taken until the program ends. One bullet is nothing; a leak every frame at 60 frames a second eats the machine.
- **Dangling pointer:** you `delete` and keep using the pointer. The memory may already belong to something else. Setting the pointer to `nullptr` after `delete` makes the mistake visible.
- **Double delete:** two parts of the code both `delete` the same object. Usually a crash, sometimes much later, far from the real bug.

All three come from the same question: **who owns this object, and who is responsible for deleting it?** With raw `new` the answer lives only in your head.

**Why modern C++ avoids raw new.** It is too easy to forget a `delete` when a function has several `return`s or an error happens halfway. Modern code lets objects clean up after themselves: `std::vector` for arrays, and smart pointers (`std::unique_ptr`, `std::shared_ptr`) for single objects. You will meet them in the next units. Unreal has its own answer (a garbage collector for `UObject`s, plus `TUniquePtr` and `TSharedPtr` for everything else). You learn `new`/`delete` here so you know what those tools do for you, and so you can read older code.

In this course's tests a class keeps a count of how many objects are **alive**: the constructor adds one, the destructor takes one away. If the count isn't back to where it started after your code runs, something leaked.

notes: new Bullet(10) builds a Bullet on the heap and gives back its address.
The alive counter goes up in the constructor and down in the destructor: it is a leak detector.
After delete, b still holds the old address; setting it to nullptr stops accidental use.
new int[n] allows a size chosen while running; it must be freed with delete[].

exercises.title: A buffer of readings
exercises.prompt:
Write int* makeReadings(int count, int start): allocate an array of count ints with new[], fill it with start, start+1, start+2, ... and return it. If count is 0 or less, return nullptr.
Write void freeReadings(int* readings) that releases an array made by makeReadings (it must be safe to call with nullptr).

tests.call: []{ int* p = makeReadings(3, 10); if (!p) return -1; int r = p[0] + p[2]; freeReadings(p); return r; }()
[]{ int* p = makeReadings(5, 0); if (!p) return -1; int r = p[4]; freeReadings(p); return r; }()

tests.why: An array made with new[] must be freed with delete[].
Allocate the array with new int[count].

hints: int* p = new int[count]; then a for loop that sets p[i] = start + i.
freeReadings is one line: delete[] readings; (delete[] on nullptr does nothing).

exercises.title: Grow an array
exercises.prompt: Write int* grow(int* old, int oldSize, int newSize): make a new array of newSize ints, copy the first min(oldSize, newSize) values from old, set any extra slots to 0, release old with delete[], and return the new array. old may be nullptr when oldSize is 0. (This is what std::vector does when it runs out of room.)

tests.call: []{ int* a = new int[2]{5, 6}; a = grow(a, 2, 4); if (!a) return -1; int r = a[0] * 1000 + a[1] * 100 + a[2] * 10 + a[3]; delete[] a; return r; }()
tests.hint_if_fail: Copy the old values, then fill the new slots with 0.

tests.call: []{ int* a = new int[3]{1, 2, 3}; a = grow(a, 3, 2); if (!a) return -1; int r = a[0] * 10 + a[1]; delete[] a; return r; }()
tests.hint_if_fail: When shrinking, copy only newSize values.

tests.call: []{ int* a = grow(nullptr, 0, 3); if (!a) return -1; int r = a[0] + a[1] + a[2]; delete[] a; return r; }()

tests.why: Release the old array with delete[] or it leaks.

hints: int* bigger = new int[newSize]; then loop i < newSize: copy old[i] when i < oldSize, else 0.
Finish with delete[] old; return bigger;

exercises.title: Spawn and despawn bullets
exercises.prompt:
Bullet is given (with a live counter). Write Bullet* spawnBullet(int damage) that creates a Bullet on the heap with new and returns it.
Write void despawn(Bullet*& b) that deletes the bullet and sets the caller's pointer to nullptr so it can't dangle. Calling it with a null pointer does nothing.

tests.call: []{ Bullet* b = spawnBullet(7); int d = b ? b->damage : -1; despawn(b); return d; }()
[]{ int before = Bullet::alive; Bullet* b = spawnBullet(5); int during = Bullet::alive - before; despawn(b); return during; }()
[]{ int before = Bullet::alive; Bullet* b = spawnBullet(5); despawn(b); return Bullet::alive - before; }()
[]{ Bullet* b = spawnBullet(5); despawn(b); return b == nullptr; }()
tests.hint_if_fail: b is a reference to the caller's pointer: set it to nullptr after delete.

tests.call: []{ Bullet* b = nullptr; despawn(b); return b == nullptr; }()

hints: despawn takes Bullet*& : a reference to a pointer, so b = nullptr changes the caller's variable.

quiz.q: int* a = new int[10]; How should it be freed?
A game news one Particle per frame and never deletes them. What happens?
choices: A memory leak that grows every frame
quiz.why: Every new needs a delete; otherwise memory piles up.

quiz.q: After delete p; what does p hold?
quiz.why: delete doesn't change p, which is why you set it to nullptr.
Deleting a null pointer is a safe no-op.

quiz.q: Why does modern C++ avoid raw new and delete?
choices: It's easy to forget a delete or delete twice; vector and smart pointers clean up automatically
quiz.why: Ownership by hand is error-prone; tools that own memory release it for you.

cards.a: T* p = new T(args); ... delete p;
T* a = new T[n]; ... delete[] a;
Leak: never deleted. Dangling: deleted but still used.

explain: Explain what a memory leak and a dangling pointer are, using bullets in a game as your example.
